rationale: This review of bilateral surgical lesions reports drooling among adverse outcomes in some clinical series. Surgery and disease features define the comparisons. No raw-fig exposure was assessed.
The article covers animal health and disease occurrence. Its scope contains no human Parkinson population or raw-fig exposure comparison.
The speech corpus records sialorrhea presence, absence and missingness for Parkinson participants. The annotation supplies no graded change or dietary exposure.
The 304 published posters include a non-Parkinson psychiatric medication case series with drooling and separate saliva sampling studies. No screened poster tests raw fig for Parkinson drooling.
The hybrid posters use saliva as a sample in several studies and report drooling in an infant genetic diagnosis. The published collection supplies no raw-fig comparison in Parkinson disease.
The review concerns experimental neuromodulation approaches. The text mentions sialorrhea as a medication adverse effect and has no culinary comparison.
Passive drooling is a saliva specimen collection method in the diagnostic biomarker study. The study does not measure clinical drooling severity or assign raw fig.
The infant feeding instrument codes dribbling milk as a behavioral cue. It does not measure Parkinson sialorrhea or raw fig.

Sialorrhea is a baseline clinical finding in a participant initially diagnosed with Parkinson disease and later classified as multiple system atrophy. The report does not compare raw fig or graded drooling.
The hemifacial spasm review describes transient drooling after medical treatment as an adverse event. No relevant dietary or Parkinson symptom comparison is reported.
The review concerns cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction and cognitive impairment in Parkinson disease. No raw-fig exposure or drooling-severity contrast is reported.
Table 2 supplies an eight-week −0.22-point drooling estimate (95% CI −1.1 to 0.7) from the remote speech-therapy trial. The study did not assign a food exposure.
The research history mentions drooling among historical descriptions. It supplies no measured raw-fig exposure or graded symptom result.
The medicinal chemistry review mentions drooling in the context of symptomatic pediatric drug treatment. It contains no raw-fig comparison in Parkinson disease.
The review describes drooling in historical Wilson disease accounts. Clinical symptom and toxicology contexts concern other exposures and diagnoses.

The official supplement contains 366 numbered entries, including ten marked withdrawn. EPR-093 compares genetic subgroups and groups sialorrhea with other nonmotor symptoms. No member supplies the exact food and outcome comparison.
The primary study addresses an infectious-disease drug-repurposing question. It does not include a Parkinson cohort or a raw-fig drooling outcome.
The masticatory muscle trial measured structural and functional temporalis outcomes. Parkinson drooling appears in cited background. The randomized comparison does not measure the claim outcome.
A cross-sectional 22q11.2 deletion study measures saliva α-synuclein concentration. Drooling is the collection method and no symptom change or food exposure is measured.
This bibliometric analysis maps publications and places drooling in a research cluster. It does not supply patient-level raw fig or symptom-change evidence.
The meta-analysis compares anesthesia approaches for DBS surgery. It discusses saliva retention in clinical context and supplies no raw-fig estimate.
The review discusses medication-related sialorrhea while comparing options for Parkinson psychosis. It contains no raw-fig comparison.
Pooled safety tables report drooling as an adverse event in non-Parkinson treatment populations. No raw fig comparison or Parkinson symptom estimate is available.
The review describes sialorrhea in Huntington disease. The population and exposures do not match the frozen claim.
Drooling is part of a multicomponent swallow screen in a nursing-home sample. The design gives no raw-fig or Parkinson-specific drooling severity result.
The neuropalliative review lists oral cueing and symptomatic clinical approaches for drooling. It reports no original raw-fig exposure comparison.
The multiple system atrophy case records sialorrhea among other clinical signs during a vocal-flutter assessment. Drooling was not graded and diet was not compared.
The progressive supranuclear palsy study includes drooling as a listed clinical feature. The comparison concerns a distinct diagnosis and no raw-fig exposure.

The official supplement includes retrospective sialorrhea and physical-activity results in separate cohorts. The physical-activity poster gives a within-group drooling p-value and its table image has no drooling between-group estimate. No screened member tests raw fig.
Drooling or frothing is one item in a marmoset model's composite clinical rating. The study compares training and transplantation conditions without raw fig or a human drooling measure.
The systematic review concerns VMAT-2 inhibitor studies in schizophrenia and psychosis. It contains no food exposure comparison or Parkinson drooling assessment.
The dementia with Lewy bodies study includes salivation and drooling among scale items. The quality-of-life analyses do not estimate change after raw-fig exposure.
The genetic association article includes drooling as introductory Parkinson context. Its analytical outcomes concern Parkinson and depression traits, with no raw fig or symptom-change comparison.
The perspective discusses saliva control and dysphagia in the scope of Parkinson allied health care. It provides no original dietary comparison.
The study discusses drooling as a possible influence on self-esteem. The measured outcomes concern sexual health rather than a dietary change in drooling.
The consensus statement describes multidisciplinary rehabilitation and clinical roles for saliva control. It supplies no measured raw-fig exposure.
The clinical perspective describes behavioral cueing and symptom management. It does not estimate the effect of raw fig.
